topic: AI, ML, deep learning, and GenAI
question: A product manager says that the company's new large language model (LLM) chatbot is "generative AI, not machine learning," so the company's ML governance process does not apply to it. Which statement correctly describes how these terms relate?
options: LLMs are ML models but not deep learning models, because the transformer architecture replaces neural networks.
Generative AI becomes ML only after the model is fine-tuned on company-specific data.
Generative AI is a separate branch of AI that relies on expert-written rules instead of learned models.
LLMs are deep learning models, deep learning is a subset of ML, and ML is a subset of AI.
explanations: The transformer is a neural network architecture. LLMs built on transformers are deep learning models.
A pre-trained foundation model is already a trained ML model. Fine-tuning is an optional customization step.
Rule-based (symbolic) AI uses hand-written rules. Generative AI models learn their parameters from very large datasets.

An LLM is a neural network whose parameters are learned from data, so it is an ML model (specifically a deep learning model). Generative AI describes what the model does (create content), not a separate non-ML technology, so ML governance applies.
takeaway: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning, and generative AI models such as LLMs are built with deep learning. GenAI is still ML and needs the same governance.

question: A company has a generative AI assistant that answers employee questions from an HR knowledge base. The company now wants a solution that can take a request such as "book my parental leave," check the leave policy, look up the employee's leave balance in the HR system, submit the request, and notify the manager. Which capability distinguishes the new solution from the existing assistant?
options: It is fine-tuned on historical leave requests so that it memorizes the workflow.
It retrieves policy passages from a vector store to ground its answers.
It uses a larger foundation model with a longer context window.
It plans multi-step actions toward a goal and calls tools or APIs to carry them out.
explanations: Fine-tuning changes how a model responds. It does not give the model authorized access to the HR system or the ability to submit a request.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds answers in documents. The existing assistant already does this, and retrieval alone does not submit requests or notify anyone.
A larger model or context window can improve answers, but it does not give the system the ability to plan steps or take actions in other systems.
Agentic AI breaks a goal into steps, decides which tools to use, acts in external systems (the HR system, notifications), and uses the results to decide the next step.
takeaway: RAG helps a model answer; agentic AI helps a system act. Agents combine a model with planning, tools, and memory to reach a goal.

question: A logistics company has millions of photos of damaged parcels. Its traditional ML approach required engineers to hand-craft image features, and accuracy has stopped improving. Which characteristic of deep learning makes it the MOST suitable next approach?
options: Deep learning models are easier to interpret than decision trees, which simplifies audits.
Neural networks with many layers learn features directly from raw, unstructured data such as images.
Deep learning models typically need less training data and less compute than traditional ML algorithms such as decision trees.
Deep learning removes the need for labeled examples when training a supervised image classifier for damage types.
explanations: Deep neural networks are generally harder to interpret than decision trees or linear models.
Deep learning learns feature representations automatically from raw pixels, audio, or text. This removes the manual feature-engineering bottleneck that limited the traditional approach.
Deep learning usually needs more data and more compute than traditional ML algorithms, not less.
Pre-training on unlabeled data can reduce labeling needs, but a supervised damage classifier still needs labeled examples of each damage type.
takeaway: Deep learning shines on large volumes of unstructured data because it learns features itself, at the cost of more data, more compute, and less interpretability.

question: During pre-training, an LLM learns by predicting the next token in billions of sentences of public text. No person labeled the data. Which type of learning does this describe?
options: Self-supervised learning, because the training targets are derived from the data itself
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), because the model is rewarded for correct predictions
Unsupervised clustering, because the model groups similar sentences without labels
Supervised learning, because human annotators provided the correct output for every example
explanations: The "label" for each position is simply the next token in the text, so the data supervises itself. This is how foundation models learn from huge unlabeled corpora.
RLHF is an alignment step that usually happens after pre-training. It uses human preference rankings to train a reward model.
The model is not grouping sentences. It predicts a specific target (the next token) for each position.
No human annotators were involved. Supervised learning relies on labels that are supplied for each example, such as a category or a target value.
takeaway: FM pre-training is self-supervised: the targets come from the unlabeled data itself. Fine-tuning and RLHF come later.

question: A payment processor has billions of historical transactions. Fewer than 0.01% are confirmed fraud, and fraudsters keep inventing schemes that do not resemble past cases. The company wants to flag transactions that look unusual compared with normal customer behavior. Which approach BEST fits this requirement?
options: Unsupervised anomaly detection that learns normal patterns and flags outliers
Linear regression that predicts the transaction amount for each customer
Supervised binary classification trained only on the confirmed fraud labels
Reinforcement learning that rewards the model each time it blocks a transaction
explanations: Anomaly detection does not depend on labels for every fraud pattern. It models normal behavior and flags deviations, so it can surface new schemes that no labeled example describes.
Regression predicts a numeric value. Predicting the amount does not by itself identify unusual behavior.
A supervised classifier learns the patterns in its labels. With very few labels, it mostly recognizes known fraud and can miss new schemes.
There is no environment or reward signal described, and rewarding blocks would encourage the model to block legitimate payments.
takeaway: Few labels plus novel patterns point to unsupervised anomaly detection. Plenty of labeled outcomes point to supervised classification.

question: A company wants software to control heating and cooling in its office buildings. The system should try different settings, observe the resulting energy cost and occupant comfort, and gradually improve its control strategy to maximize long-term savings. Which type of ML fits this requirement?
options: Transfer learning
Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
explanations: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on one task for a related task. It does not describe learning by trial and reward.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data. It does not learn a sequence of actions from feedback.
Supervised learning needs labeled examples of the correct setting for each situation. The company does not have these; it wants the system to discover them.
An agent takes actions in an environment, receives rewards (lower cost, acceptable comfort), and improves its policy to maximize cumulative reward. This is reinforcement learning.
takeaway: Agent + environment + actions + reward over time = reinforcement learning.

question: A news publisher wants to tag each article with every relevant topic from a fixed list of 25 topics. An article about an electric-vehicle subsidy could be tagged Politics, Automotive, and Energy. Which ML task is this?
options: Clustering
Named entity recognition
Multiclass classification
Multi-label classification
explanations: Clustering discovers groups without predefined labels. Here, the 25 topics are known in advance.
Named entity recognition extracts mentions such as people, places, and organizations. It does not assign topic labels to a whole article.
Multiclass classification assigns exactly one class from several options. This task needs several labels per article.
Each article can receive any number of labels from a predefined set. That is multi-label classification.
takeaway: One label from many = multiclass. Several labels at once = multi-label. No predefined labels = clustering.

question: A subscription company wants a model that outputs, for each customer, the probability (from 0 to 1) that the customer will cancel within the next 30 days. The company will contact customers whose probability is above 0.7. Which type of ML problem is this?
options: Binary classification
Regression, because the model outputs a continuous number
Time-series forecasting, because the prediction covers a future 30-day window
Clustering, because customers are split into contact and no-contact groups
explanations: The outcome has two classes. Many classifiers output a class probability, and the business chooses a threshold (0.7) to turn it into a decision.
The target being predicted is yes or no (cancels or not). The probability is a confidence score for that class. Regression predicts a continuous target such as revenue.
Forecasting predicts future values of a series, such as next month's demand. This predicts a yes/no outcome for each customer.
The two groups come from a threshold on a predicted label, not from structure discovered in unlabeled data.
takeaway: Look at the target: a yes/no outcome is classification even if the model outputs a probability. A quantity is regression.

question: An insurer trains a model that predicts the dollar amount of each new claim. Which TWO metrics are appropriate for evaluating this model? (Select TWO.)
options: Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
F1 score
Mean absolute error (MAE)
Precision
Root mean squared error (RMSE)
explanations: AUC measures how well a classifier separates classes across thresholds. It does not apply to a continuous target.
F1 combines precision and recall for classification. The claim amount is a continuous value.
MAE is the average absolute difference between predicted and actual amounts, expressed in dollars.
Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct. It applies to classification.
RMSE measures the typical size of prediction errors for a numeric target and penalizes large errors more heavily.
takeaway: Numeric target → regression metrics (RMSE, MAE, R²). Classes → accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC.

question: A retailer wants to divide 2 million loyalty-program members into groups with similar purchasing behavior so that marketers can design a campaign for each group. The retailer has no predefined segment labels. Which technique should the retailer use?
options: Multiclass classification
Principal component analysis (PCA)
Linear regression
K-means clustering
explanations: Classification needs labeled examples of each segment. The retailer has no predefined segments.
PCA is unsupervised, but it reduces the number of features. It does not assign customers to segments.
Regression predicts a numeric value. It does not group customers.
Clustering groups similar records in unlabeled data. Marketers can then inspect and name the discovered segments.
takeaway: Unlabeled data + find natural groups → clustering. Dimensionality reduction (PCA) is a different job.

question: A manufacturer collects vibration readings from each machine every second and stores them with timestamps. Technicians also write free-text notes describing each repair. Which TWO statements correctly describe this data? (Select TWO.)
options: The vibration readings are unstructured data because sensors generate them continuously.
The technicians' notes are labeled data because a person wrote them.
The vibration readings are time-series data because their order in time carries meaning.
Both datasets become tabular data once they are stored in Amazon S3.
The technicians' notes are unstructured data.
explanations: Timestamped numeric readings have a fixed schema, so they are structured, even when they arrive continuously.
Being written by a person does not make text a label. A label is the target value that a model is trained to predict.
Values recorded at regular time intervals, where sequence and timing matter, are time-series data.
The storage location does not change the nature of the data. S3 stores structured and unstructured objects alike.
Free-form text has no predefined schema, so it is unstructured data (like images, audio, and video).
takeaway: Classify data by its shape and meaning, not by where it is stored. Ordered timestamps = time series; free text, images, and audio = unstructured.

question: A company has 500,000 unlabeled images of manufactured parts and wants to train a defect-detection model. It needs a managed way to label the images using its own employees and a third-party vendor workforce, with automated labeling to reduce cost. Which AWS service should the company use?
options: Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I)
Amazon SageMaker Clarify
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
explanations: Amazon A2I adds human review of model predictions in production, for example low-confidence results. It is not designed to build large labeled training datasets.
Clarify detects bias and explains predictions. It does not label data.
Rekognition Custom Labels trains an image model from labeled images. It is not designed to run large labeling jobs across private and vendor workforces.
Ground Truth creates labeled training datasets using private, vendor, or public workforces, and it can use automated data labeling to reduce labeling cost.
takeaway: Build labeled training data → SageMaker Ground Truth. Human review of live predictions → Amazon A2I.

question: A media company hosts a custom model on Amazon SageMaker AI that analyzes uploaded video files. Each file can be up to 800 MB, and processing takes 5 to 20 minutes. Users are notified when their results are ready. The company wants the endpoint to scale in to zero instances when there are no requests. Which inference option should the company use?
options: Real-time inference
Asynchronous inference
Serverless inference
Batch transform
explanations: Real-time endpoints are built for interactive, low-latency requests with small payloads and short processing times. Large files that take up to 20 minutes do not fit this pattern.
Asynchronous inference queues requests, supports large payloads (up to 1 GB) and long processing times (up to 1 hour), can notify on completion, and can scale in to zero instances.
Serverless inference suits small, short requests with idle periods. Its payload size and processing time limits are far below 800 MB and 20 minutes.
Batch transform runs offline jobs over a whole dataset. It is not designed to respond to individual uploads as they arrive.
takeaway: Large payloads, long processing, near-real-time results, scale to zero → SageMaker asynchronous inference.

question: A startup deploys a small text-classification model that receives a few hundred requests during business hours and almost none overnight or on weekends. Requests are small, and some extra latency on the first request after an idle period is acceptable. The startup wants to minimize cost and avoid managing instances. Which SageMaker AI inference option BEST meets these requirements?
options: Real-time inference with one always-on instance
Batch transform
Asynchronous inference
Serverless inference
explanations: An always-on instance is billed during nights and weekends when there is almost no traffic.
Batch transform runs scheduled offline jobs. It does not return predictions to individual requests on demand.
Asynchronous inference queues requests and writes results to Amazon S3. It is designed for large payloads and long processing, which adds complexity here.
Serverless inference manages capacity for you, scales with traffic, and charges for compute used. It suits intermittent traffic that can tolerate cold starts.
takeaway: Intermittent traffic + tolerates cold starts + no instance management → serverless inference.

question: A bank must score its entire portfolio of 12 million loans for default risk at the end of each month. The results are loaded into a data warehouse the next morning. No application requests predictions between runs. Which SageMaker AI inference option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Real-time inference
Serverless inference
Asynchronous inference
Batch transform
explanations: A persistent real-time endpoint would be billed all month even though it is used only once.
Serverless inference is invoked per request. Sending 12 million individual requests is inefficient compared with a single batch job.
Asynchronous inference handles individual queued requests through an endpoint. Scoring a complete dataset on a schedule is what batch transform is built for.
Batch transform processes a whole dataset as a job, provisions compute only while the job runs, and writes results to Amazon S3. No persistent endpoint is needed.
takeaway: Score a whole dataset on a schedule, no endpoint needed → batch transform.

question: An online store must return a fraud score within 100 milliseconds while the customer waits at checkout. Traffic is steady throughout the day and night. Which SageMaker AI inference option should the company choose?
options: Asynchronous inference
Serverless inference
Batch transform
Real-time inference
explanations: Asynchronous inference queues requests and delivers results later. The checkout cannot wait.
Serverless inference can add cold-start latency and is designed for intermittent traffic. Steady traffic with strict latency needs a real-time endpoint.
Batch transform scores data offline and cannot respond during a live checkout.
Real-time endpoints are persistent, fully managed endpoints for interactive, low-latency predictions, which fits steady checkout traffic.
takeaway: Interactive, low-latency, steady traffic → real-time endpoint. Order of latency: real-time < asynchronous < batch.

question: A model that classifies support tickets reaches 99% accuracy on its training data but only 72% on a validation set drawn from the same period. Which action is MOST likely to improve the model's performance on new tickets?
options: Train on the validation set as well and report training accuracy
Add more layers and parameters to the model
Train for more epochs until training accuracy reaches 100%
Add more diverse training examples and apply regularization or early stopping
explanations: Removing the held-out set hides the problem. The team would no longer have an honest estimate of performance on new data.
Extra capacity makes it easier to memorize the training data, which worsens overfitting.
More training on the same data increases memorization and usually widens the gap between training and validation accuracy.
The large gap indicates overfitting. More varied data and techniques that limit memorization (regularization, early stopping) help the model generalize.
takeaway: High training score + much lower validation score = overfitting (high variance). Fix with more/diverse data, regularization, early stopping, or a simpler model.

question: A data scientist trains a linear model to predict delivery times. The model scores poorly on the training data and on the validation data, and the errors on each are similar. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: The model is overfitting because it memorized noise in the training data instead of general patterns.
The model is underfitting because it is too simple to capture the patterns in the data.
Information from the validation set leaked into the training set during feature preparation.
The model is experiencing data drift in production.
explanations: An overfit model performs well on training data. Here, training performance is also poor.
Poor accuracy on both training and validation data indicates high bias. The model needs more informative features or a more expressive algorithm.
Leakage makes evaluation results look better than they should. It does not explain poor results on both sets.
Drift describes production data changing after deployment. This problem appears during training.
takeaway: Poor on training AND validation → underfitting (high bias). Good on training, poor on validation → overfitting (high variance).

question: A government agency must calculate each citizen's benefit amount by using a formula defined in legislation. Auditors require that identical inputs always produce identical, fully traceable results. A vendor proposes an ML model trained on 10 years of past calculations. What should the agency do?
options: Fine-tune a foundation model on the legislation so that it can compute the amounts.
Use the ML model and explain each result with feature attributions.
Implement the published formula in rule-based software instead of using ML.
Use the ML model and set its temperature to 0 so that results are deterministic.
explanations: A fine-tuned model is still probabilistic. It cannot guarantee exact results for every case.
Explanations describe how a model reached a prediction. They do not make an approximation match the law exactly.
When the rules are known and a specific, exact outcome is required, conventional deterministic code is more accurate, cheaper, and fully auditable.
Temperature is a sampling setting for generative models. Even with repeatable outputs, a learned model only approximates the legal formula and can be wrong.
takeaway: ML produces predictions, not guaranteed outcomes. When the logic is known and exactness is required, use conventional code.

question: A small law firm receives about 30 contract amendments per month. A paralegal classifies each one in about two minutes with near-perfect accuracy. A consultant proposes building and maintaining a custom ML classifier. Which consideration MOST strongly indicates that ML is NOT appropriate here?
options: ML models cannot classify legal documents because legal language is too complex.
The firm would need to use unsupervised learning because it has no labeled data.
The cost to build and maintain the model would exceed the value of the time it saves.
Classification models require millions of labeled examples before they are useful.
explanations: NLP models are widely used to classify legal text, so this is not the limiting factor.
The paralegal's past classifications could serve as labels, so supervised learning is possible.
About one hour of work per month, already done accurately, cannot justify development, hosting, monitoring, and retraining costs.
Transfer learning and pre-trained models can work with far fewer examples, so data volume alone is not the reason.
takeaway: ML must pay for itself. Low volume, accurate manual work, and ongoing maintenance costs often make a cost-benefit analysis reject ML.

question: An insurance company receives thousands of scanned claim forms each day. It must extract printed and handwritten values from specific form fields and tables while preserving which value belongs to which field. Which AWS service meets this requirement with the LEAST development effort?
options: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Textract
Amazon Kendra
explanations: Rekognition can detect text in images and video frames, but it does not return form key-value pairs or table structure.
Comprehend analyzes text that you already have, for example to find entities or sentiment. It cannot read scanned images.
Textract extracts printed and handwritten text, form key-value pairs, and tables from scanned documents and images.
Kendra is an intelligent search service. It indexes documents for search but does not return form fields as structured data.
takeaway: Documents (forms, tables, handwriting) → Textract. Images and video scenes → Rekognition. Text you already have → Comprehend.

question: Only 0.5% of a retailer's product returns are fraudulent. A new model labels every return as legitimate and reports 99.5% accuracy. The retailer considers both missed fraud and false alarms costly. Which metric should the team use to compare candidate models?
options: Mean absolute error (MAE)
Accuracy
Precision alone
F1 score for the fraud class
explanations: MAE evaluates regression models that predict numeric values.
With 99.5% legitimate returns, a model that never flags fraud still scores 99.5% accuracy. Accuracy hides the failure.
Precision ignores missed fraud. A model that flags only one obvious case can have perfect precision and still miss almost all fraud.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it balances false alarms against missed fraud. It is also meaningful when classes are imbalanced.
takeaway: Imbalanced classes make accuracy misleading. Recall = how much fraud is caught; precision = how many alerts are real; F1 balances both.

question: A healthcare provider wants to extract medications, dosages, and medical conditions from unstructured clinical notes and link them to standard codes such as ICD-10-CM and RxNorm. The provider does not want to build or train its own model. Which AWS service should the provider use?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Comprehend Medical
Amazon Transcribe Medical
explanations: Textract extracts text from scanned documents. It does not understand medical meaning or assign medical codes.
Comprehend detects general entities such as people, places, and organizations. It does not extract medical entities or link them to medical ontologies without custom training.
Comprehend Medical is a HIPAA-eligible NLP service that extracts medical information such as conditions, medications, and dosages and links it to ICD-10-CM, RxNorm, and SNOMED CT.
Transcribe Medical converts medical speech into text. The clinical notes are already text.
takeaway: Medical NLP on text (conditions, medications, ICD-10-CM/RxNorm codes) → Comprehend Medical. Medical speech → Transcribe Medical.

question: A contact center stores recordings of customer calls in Amazon S3. Managers want to know which calls contain negative customer sentiment and which products customers mention, without building custom ML models. Which TWO AWS services should the company combine? (Select TWO.)
options: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Lex
Amazon Polly
explanations: Rekognition analyzes images and video, not audio.
Comprehend analyzes the transcripts for sentiment and entities such as product names.
Transcribe converts the recorded speech into text so that it can be analyzed.
Lex builds conversational bots. It does not analyze stored call recordings.
Polly converts text into speech, which is the opposite direction.
takeaway: Speech → text with Transcribe, then text → insights (sentiment, entities, key phrases) with Comprehend.

question: A bank wants customers to check balances and report lost cards through a chatbot on its website and through its phone line. The solution must recognize what the customer wants, ask for missing details such as the last four digits of the card, and then call a backend function. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Lex
Amazon Polly
explanations: Comprehend analyzes text for sentiment and entities. It does not manage multi-turn conversations or fulfill requests.
Transcribe converts speech to text. It does not recognize intents or manage slot-filling dialog.
Lex builds voice and text conversational interfaces. It recognizes intents, collects required details (slots) through multi-turn dialog, and can invoke a function to fulfill the request.
Polly generates lifelike speech from text. It does not understand intent or manage a conversation.
takeaway: Intents + slots + multi-turn dialog + fulfillment, by voice or text → Amazon Lex.

question: A company uses Amazon Polly to read product announcements aloud. Polly consistently mispronounces the company's invented brand names and several industry acronyms. The company wants the correct pronunciation to apply automatically to every future announcement. What should the company do?
options: Add the brand names to an Amazon Transcribe custom vocabulary.
Switch to a different Amazon Polly voice for each announcement.
Create an Amazon Translate custom terminology file for the brand names.
Upload a pronunciation lexicon to Amazon Polly and apply it during speech synthesis.
explanations: A Transcribe custom vocabulary improves speech-to-text recognition. It has no effect on how Polly speaks.
Changing voices does not teach Polly how to pronounce specific words, and the problem would persist.
Custom terminology controls how terms are translated between languages, not how they are pronounced.
Lexicons define how specific words and acronyms are pronounced and are applied automatically when you synthesize speech. SSML phoneme tags are a per-message alternative.
takeaway: Polly lexicons control how text is spoken. Transcribe custom vocabularies control how speech is recognized. Translate custom terminology controls translation.

question: A pharmaceutical company transcribes recorded sales meetings with Amazon Transcribe. The transcripts frequently misspell drug names and internal project code names. Which solution will improve transcription accuracy for these specific terms with the LEAST effort?
options: Add the terms to an Amazon Polly pronunciation lexicon.
Train a custom speech recognition model from scratch on Amazon SageMaker AI.
Create a custom vocabulary in Amazon Transcribe that lists the drug and project names.
Use Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition on the finished transcripts.
explanations: Polly lexicons affect text-to-speech output, not speech recognition.
Building an ASR model from scratch requires far more data and effort than a custom vocabulary.
Custom vocabularies tell Transcribe how to recognize specific words, such as product names and jargon, that it would otherwise mishear.
Custom entity recognition finds entities in text. It does not correct words that were transcribed incorrectly.
takeaway: Specific terms misrecognized → Transcribe custom vocabulary. Broad domain language → Transcribe custom language model.

question: A company wants to add text summarization to an internal application. It has no ML operations team, expects unpredictable request volume, and wants to pay only for what it uses. Another team suggests hosting an open-weight model on Amazon EC2 GPU instances. What is the PRIMARY advantage of using a managed API such as Amazon Bedrock instead?
options: Inference costs are fixed each month regardless of how many requests the company sends.
The company gets full control of the model weights, serving container, and instance types.
The company can modify the model's internal architecture before each request.
AWS manages the serving infrastructure and scaling, and on-demand usage is billed per token.
explanations: On-demand pricing is based on input and output tokens, so costs vary with usage.
This is an advantage of self-hosting, not of a managed API.
A managed API gives access to the model through an API. It does not expose the model architecture for modification.
With a managed API, the company calls the model without provisioning, patching, or scaling servers, and on-demand pricing follows actual usage.
takeaway: Managed API (Bedrock): no infrastructure, pay per token, fast start. Self-hosted (EC2 or SageMaker AI endpoints): full control, but you manage and pay for provisioned capacity.

question: A video-streaming company wants to show each viewer a list of recommended titles that updates in real time as the viewer watches content. The company has user-interaction data but little ML expertise. Which AWS service is the MOST appropriate?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon Personalize
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
explanations: OpenSearch Service powers search, including semantic search. It does not learn personalized rankings from user-interaction history on its own.
Canvas builds no-code predictive models on tabular data. It is not a managed real-time recommendation service.
Personalize is a fully managed service that trains recommendation models on user-item interaction data and returns real-time personalized recommendations.
Knowledge Bases retrieve document passages for RAG. They do not produce recommendations from viewing behavior.
takeaway: Personalized recommendations from interaction data, in real time, with little ML expertise → Amazon Personalize.

question: A lender must approve or deny small-business loans by using 40 structured fields from each application. Regulators require the lender to tell each rejected applicant the specific factors that drove the decision. Each decision must be returned in under 50 milliseconds. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?
options: Build a RAG application that retrieves the lending policy for every application.
Train a traditional ML model on the tabular data and explain each decision with feature attributions.
Fine-tune a foundation model on past loan decisions so that it writes a decision letter that lists the reasons.
Send each application to an LLM and ask it to explain, step by step, which factors drove its approval decision.
explanations: RAG supplies policy text to a generative model. It does not produce a validated risk prediction or reasons tied to the applicant's fields.
Traditional models, such as gradient-boosted trees, work well on structured data, run in milliseconds, and support per-decision feature attributions (for example, SHAP values from SageMaker Clarify).
A fine-tuned FM remains difficult to interpret. The reasons it writes are generated text, not faithful, feature-level explanations of how it decided.
An LLM's generated explanation might not reflect how the decision was actually made. LLM calls also add latency and cost, which makes the 50 ms target hard to meet.
takeaway: Structured data + explainability requirements + tight latency → traditional ML with feature attributions. FMs suit open-ended, unstructured, generative tasks.

question: A company is deciding between traditional ML models and foundation models (FMs) for several new projects. Which TWO project requirements favor an FM? (Select TWO.)
options: Flagging fraudulent card transactions in under 10 milliseconds with explainable features
Estimating house prices from 20 property attributes in a model that regulators audit
Answering open-ended employee questions about hundreds of unstructured policy documents
Predicting next quarter's sales for each store from five years of tabular sales history
Drafting personalized email replies in 12 languages from short bullet-point notes
explanations: Strict latency and explainability requirements on structured data favor traditional ML models.
A regression model on structured attributes is simpler to validate, explain, and audit.
Understanding unstructured documents and generating answers to open-ended questions is an FM task, often combined with RAG.
Forecasting from structured history is a well-defined task for traditional forecasting or regression models.
Generating fluent text in many languages with little task-specific training data is a strength of FMs.
takeaway: FMs: open-ended, generative, language or multimodal tasks with little labeled data. Traditional ML: narrow predictions on structured data with strict latency, cost, or explainability needs.

question: Business analysts at a retailer want to build a model that predicts which customers will respond to a promotion, using a CSV file of past campaign results. They have no coding or ML experience and want to generate predictions themselves through a visual interface. Which AWS service should they use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker AI training jobs launched with the SageMaker Python SDK
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
explanations: Ground Truth creates labeled datasets. It does not train or deploy predictive models.
Training jobs through the SDK require writing code, which the analysts cannot do.
JumpStart provides pre-trained models and solution templates for ML practitioners. It is not a no-code tool for training a prediction model on a CSV file.
Canvas is a visual, no-code interface for preparing data, building ML models, and generating predictions without writing code.
takeaway: No-code ML for business analysts → SageMaker Canvas.

question: A team is planning its first ML project. Which sequence lists the stages of the ML development lifecycle in the correct order?
options: Data collection → data preprocessing and feature engineering → model training → model evaluation → deployment → monitoring
Data preprocessing and feature engineering → data collection → model evaluation → model training → deployment → monitoring
Data collection → model training → data preprocessing and feature engineering → deployment → model evaluation → monitoring
Data collection → data preprocessing and feature engineering → model evaluation → model training → monitoring → deployment
explanations: Data is collected and prepared, a model is trained (and tuned), evaluated against success criteria, deployed, and then monitored so that it can be retrained when needed.
You cannot prepare data before collecting it, and you cannot evaluate a model before training it.
Data must be cleaned and features engineered before training, and a model should be evaluated before it is deployed.
Evaluation follows training, and monitoring applies to a model after it is deployed.
takeaway: Frame the business problem → collect → prepare and engineer features → train and tune → evaluate → deploy → monitor, then loop back to retrain.

question: Several data science teams compute the same customer features, such as 90-day spend, in different ways. Models perform worse in production because the features used during inference differ from those used during training. Which SageMaker AI capability addresses this problem?
options: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Clarify
explanations: Feature Store is a central repository for storing, sharing, and reusing features, with offline storage for training and online storage for low-latency inference, which keeps them consistent.
Model Registry catalogs and approves model versions. It does not store or serve features.
Ground Truth labels data. It does not provide consistent features to training and inference.
Clarify detects bias and explains predictions. It does not manage feature definitions.
takeaway: Consistent, reusable features across teams and between training and inference → SageMaker Feature Store.

question: An ML platform team wants to catalog every trained model version with its evaluation metrics and require a manager to set a version's status to Approved before a CI/CD pipeline can deploy it to production. Which SageMaker AI capability is designed for this?
options: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
explanations: Feature Store manages features, not model versions.
Model Monitor checks the quality of models that are already deployed.
Model Registry organizes model versions in model groups, stores their metadata and metrics, and tracks an approval status that deployment pipelines can use as a gate.
Model Cards document a model's intended uses, risk rating, and evaluation results for governance. They are not a versioned catalog that gates CI/CD deployments.
takeaway: Model Registry = versions + approval status + deployment handoff. Model Cards = governance documentation.

question: A credit-scoring model deployed on a SageMaker AI endpoint has become less accurate since the company launched a product for younger customers. Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor reports that the distributions of several input features now differ significantly from the training baseline. What should the company do NEXT?
options: Roll back to the previous model version, which had better accuracy when it was first deployed.
Raise the Model Monitor thresholds so that the violations stop.
Retrain the model on recent, representative data, evaluate it, and redeploy it if it performs better.
Increase the endpoint instance size and enable auto scaling so that the model can handle the new customers.
explanations: The previous version was trained on even older data and does not represent the new customer population either.
Changing thresholds hides the drift. The model would continue to make worse predictions.
Model Monitor detected data drift. The MLOps response is to retrain on current data, compare against the production model, and redeploy through a controlled process.
More capacity and auto scaling improve throughput. They do not fix predictions made on data that differs from the training data.
takeaway: Model Monitor detects data quality, model quality, bias, and attribution drift. The response is to retrain on current data, validate, and redeploy, ideally through an automated pipeline.

question: A fraud model's input feature distributions look the same as they did during training. However, fraudsters have changed tactics, so transactions with the same features are now fraudulent more often than before. The model's precision and recall have dropped. Which issue does this describe?
options: Data drift, because the distribution of the input features has shifted
Concept drift, because the relationship between the inputs and the target has changed
Data leakage, because the training data included information from the future
Overfitting, because the model memorized the training data
explanations: The scenario states that the input distributions have not changed.
The same inputs now map to different outcomes. The pattern the model learned no longer holds, which is concept drift.
Leakage inflates offline evaluation results. It does not explain a decline after deployment.
Overfitting shows up as a gap between training and validation performance before deployment. This degradation happened over time in production.
takeaway: Data drift: the inputs change. Concept drift: the input-to-outcome relationship changes. Both call for monitoring with ground-truth labels and retraining.

question: A company's data scientists train models manually in notebooks, and nobody can reproduce last year's production model. Which TWO practices will MOST improve repeatability and production readiness? (Select TWO.)
options: Retrain the production model every night whether or not its performance has changed.
Use larger training instances so that each experiment finishes faster.
Build automated pipelines that record the data version, code, and parameters for each training run.
Let each data scientist deploy directly from a notebook to reduce hand-offs.
Register each model version with its evaluation metrics before it can be approved for deployment.
explanations: Retraining without evaluation gates or monitoring signals adds cost and risk, and it does not make past models reproducible.
Faster training does not make results reproducible or production-ready.
Automated, versioned pipelines (for example, SageMaker Pipelines) make each training run repeatable and traceable.
Manual notebook deployments are hard to reproduce and review, and they add technical debt.
A model registry keeps lineage and metrics for every version and gives deployments a controlled approval step.
takeaway: MLOps = automated, versioned pipelines + model registry + monitoring and retraining triggers.

question: A hospital uses a model to flag chest X-rays that might show early-stage lung disease so that a radiologist reviews them. Missing a true case is far more harmful than sending an extra healthy X-ray for review. Which metric should the hospital prioritize when selecting a model?
options: Recall
Specificity
Precision
Accuracy
explanations: Recall (sensitivity) is the share of actual cases that the model flags. Maximizing recall minimizes missed diagnoses.
Specificity measures how many healthy X-rays are correctly cleared. It does not focus on catching every true case.
Precision focuses on how many flagged X-rays are true cases. It is the priority when false positives are the costly error.
With few positive cases, a model can be highly accurate while still missing many of them.
takeaway: Costly false negatives → prioritize recall. Costly false positives → prioritize precision. Both → F1.

question: A company deployed an ML model that routes customer support tickets to the right team. The model's F1 score improved from 0.81 to 0.88. Leadership wants to know whether the project is delivering business value. Which TWO metrics should the company report? (Select TWO.)
options: Average inference latency of the endpoint
Validation loss of the latest training run
Change in the average time to resolve a ticket
Support cost per ticket compared with before deployment
Precision on the held-out validation set
explanations: Latency is an operational metric for the service. It does not show whether the business benefited.
Validation loss is a training metric with no direct business meaning.
Faster resolution is a direct operational outcome of better routing.
Cost per ticket connects the model to financial value and return on investment.
Precision is a model metric. It shows technical quality, not business impact.
takeaway: Model metrics (F1, precision, loss) show technical quality. Business metrics (cost per ticket, resolution time, ROI, customer feedback) show value.

question: A developer counts 750 English words in a prompt and assumes it will use 750 tokens. When the developer sends the same prompt to two different models on Amazon Bedrock, each model reports a different input token count, and both counts are higher than 750. What explains this?
options: Each model counts characters instead of words, so the counts equal the number of letters in the prompt.
Each model uses its own tokenizer, and a token can be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation.
Amazon Bedrock adds the output tokens to the input token count before reporting it.
Token counts depend on the temperature setting, which differed between the two requests.
explanations: Tokens are neither words nor characters. They are sub-word units defined by each model's tokenizer.
Tokenizers split text differently, and many words become several tokens. The same text can therefore produce different token counts, and different costs, on different models.
Input and output tokens are counted and billed separately.
Temperature changes how the next token is sampled. It does not change how the input text is split into tokens.
takeaway: Tokens are not words. Tokenizers differ by model, so the same text can cost different amounts on different models.

question: A company is estimating the monthly on-demand cost of a summarization feature on Amazon Bedrock. Each request sends a 4,000-token document and returns a 300-token summary. Which statement about how the company will be charged is correct?
options: The company pays only for output tokens, because input tokens are free with on-demand pricing.
The company pays a flat fee per request, so document length does not affect cost.
The company pays separately for input and output tokens at model-specific rates, and output tokens usually cost more.
The company pays an hourly rate for dedicated model capacity while the feature is enabled, regardless of how many requests it sends.
explanations: Input tokens are billed. For this workload, the 4,000 input tokens are most of the volume.
On-demand pricing is based on tokens, so longer documents cost more.
On-demand pricing charges for input tokens and output tokens at rates that vary by model and Region. Output tokens are typically priced higher.
Hourly billing for reserved model units describes Provisioned Throughput, not on-demand usage.
takeaway: On-demand = price per input token + price per output token, set per model. Long prompts and long responses both drive cost.

question: An application sends the same 6,000-token system prompt, containing product policies and formatting rules, with every request. Only the 50-token user question changes. The company wants to reduce both cost and latency without changing the model. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable prompt caching for the repeated prompt prefix on a supported model.
Increase the temperature so the model generates responses faster.
Lower the maximum output tokens setting.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model.
explanations: Prompt caching lets the model reuse a repeated prefix instead of reprocessing it. Cached input tokens are billed at a reduced rate, and response time improves.
Temperature controls randomness. It does not affect speed or the number of input tokens.
Output is a small share of the tokens here, and cutting it risks truncating answers. It does not address the repeated 6,000-token prefix.
Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for an hourly commitment. The model still processes the full prompt on every request.
takeaway: A large prompt prefix repeated across requests → prompt caching lowers input cost and latency on supported models.

question: A RAG application built on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base returns incomplete answers. The procedures in the source manuals span several paragraphs, but each retrieved chunk contains only one or two sentences, so key steps are missing from the context. Which change is MOST likely to help?
options: Reduce the chunk size further so that each retrieved chunk matches the question more precisely.
Increase the temperature so that the model fills in the missing steps.
Switch to an embeddings model that produces vectors with fewer dimensions to speed up similarity search.
Use larger chunks or hierarchical chunking so that each procedure stays together.
explanations: Smaller chunks would split the procedures into even more pieces.
A higher temperature makes the model more likely to invent steps, not recover the real ones.
Fewer dimensions reduce storage but can reduce retrieval quality. They do not keep procedures intact.
Chunks that keep a whole procedure (or parent context) together give the model the complete information it needs.
takeaway: Chunk size trades precision for context. Too small fragments ideas; too large dilutes relevance and uses more tokens. Hierarchical and semantic chunking keep related content together.

question: A support portal's keyword search fails when customers type "laptop won't turn on" because the relevant article is titled "Notebook does not power up." Which technique will let the search match these phrases by meaning?
options: Convert queries and articles into embeddings and search by vector similarity.
Increase the number of results that the keyword search returns for each query.
Normalize spelling with regular-expression rules.
Add synonyms such as "notebook" and "laptop" to each article's metadata tags.
explanations: Embeddings place text with similar meaning close together in vector space, so "laptop" and "notebook" can match even without shared keywords.
More keyword results add noise without matching synonyms.
Normalization fixes variations of the same word. It does not connect different words with the same meaning.
Manual synonym tags are still exact matching and cannot anticipate every way that customers phrase a problem.
takeaway: Embeddings map text to vectors that capture meaning. Nearby vectors = similar meaning = semantic search.

question: A team is building semantic search on Amazon Bedrock. It needs a model that converts each document chunk and each user query into a numeric vector for storage and similarity search. Which type of model should the team select?
options: A reranker model that scores retrieved passages against the query
A text generation model that writes a summary of each chunk
A text embeddings model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2
An image generation model, such as Amazon Nova Canvas
explanations: A reranker reorders results that were already retrieved. It does not create the vectors that are stored.
A text generation model produces text, not vectors for a similarity index.
Embeddings models output vectors that represent meaning. These vectors are stored in a vector index and compared by similarity.
Nova Canvas generates and edits images. It does not produce text embeddings.
takeaway: Embeddings model → vectors for storage and search. Reranker → reorder retrieved results. Text generation model → write the answer.

question: Which mechanism lets transformer-based LLMs weigh the relevance of every token in the input to every other token and process the sequence in parallel during training?
options: Iterative denoising that starts from random noise
Recurrence, which processes one token at a time and passes a hidden state forward
Self-attention
Convolution over fixed-size windows of neighboring tokens
explanations: Iterative denoising describes how diffusion models generate images.
Recurrent neural networks process tokens sequentially, which limits parallel training and long-range context.
Self-attention computes how much each token should attend to every other token, capturing long-range relationships and allowing parallel computation.
Convolutions capture local patterns within a window. They do not directly relate all tokens to each other.
takeaway: Transformers rely on self-attention. RNNs are sequential; diffusion models denoise; CNNs look at local windows.

question: A marketing team uses a model that starts from random noise and refines it over many steps, guided by a text prompt, until a product image emerges. Which type of generative model is this?
options: Generative adversarial network (GAN)
Variational autoencoder (VAE)
Autoregressive transformer language model
Diffusion model
explanations: A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator and typically produces an image in a single forward pass, not by iterative denoising.
A VAE encodes data into a latent distribution and decodes samples from it. It does not describe step-by-step denoising guided by a prompt.
An autoregressive language model generates text one token at a time.
Diffusion models learn to reverse a noising process. At generation time they start from noise and remove it step by step, guided by the prompt.
takeaway: Noise → iterative denoising = diffusion. Generator versus discriminator = GAN. Next-token prediction = autoregressive LLM.

question: An insurance company wants customers to upload a photo of vehicle damage with a short written description. The application must return a written assessment of the visible damage. The company wants to use a single model with the LEAST development effort. Which type of model should the company choose?
options: A multimodal model that accepts image and text input and produces text output
A multimodal embeddings model that converts the photo and description into one vector
A text-only LLM that receives the customer's description
An image generation model that creates a repaired version of the vehicle
explanations: A multimodal FM can reason over the photo and the description together and write the assessment in one call.
An embedding is a numeric representation. It does not produce a written assessment.
A text-only model cannot see the photo, so it would ignore the most important evidence.
Image generation produces images. The requirement is to analyze an image and produce text.
takeaway: Match the model to the modalities: image + text in, text out → a multimodal FM (for example, Amazon Nova Lite or Pro).

question: Which sequence correctly orders the stages of the foundation model (FM) lifecycle?
options: Data selection → model selection → pre-training → fine-tuning → evaluation → deployment → feedback
Data selection → pre-training → deployment → fine-tuning → model selection → evaluation → feedback
Model selection → deployment → data selection → pre-training → evaluation → fine-tuning → feedback
Pre-training → data selection → evaluation → model selection → fine-tuning → feedback → deployment
explanations: Data and model architecture are chosen first, the model is pre-trained and then fine-tuned, evaluated, deployed, and improved through feedback.
Evaluation must happen before deployment, and model selection comes before training.
A model cannot be deployed before it has been trained and evaluated.
Pre-training requires data that has already been selected, and feedback comes from a deployed model.
takeaway: FM lifecycle: data selection → model selection → pre-training → fine-tuning → evaluation → deployment → feedback, which loops back.

question: A company's leadership asks why the ML team plans to customize an existing foundation model instead of pre-training a new one. Which statement BEST explains the difference?
options: Pre-training needs only a small labeled dataset, while fine-tuning needs billions of unlabeled documents to adjust the model.
Pre-training is the only reliable way to give a model company-specific facts, such as prices and policies, that change every day.
Pre-training and fine-tuning cost about the same, but pre-training produces lower-quality models.
Pre-training learns general capabilities from massive datasets and needs far more data, compute, and cost than adapting a model.
explanations: This is reversed. Pre-training uses huge unlabeled corpora; fine-tuning uses much smaller, task-specific labeled datasets.
Frequently changing facts are best supplied at inference time with RAG. Retraining a model daily is impractical.
Pre-training costs far more than fine-tuning, and it is not inherently lower quality.
Pre-training is the most resource-intensive stage of the FM lifecycle and is usually done by model providers. Customers typically adapt existing models.
takeaway: Pre-training is the most expensive stage and is usually done by providers. Customers usually prompt, use RAG, or fine-tune.

question: An AI agent helps analysts investigate incidents in sessions that last several hours. As a session grows, the agent's answers become slower, more expensive, and less focused, because every tool result and message is appended to the prompt. Which approach BEST addresses this issue?
options: Increase the maximum output tokens so that the agent can write more complete answers.
Switch to a model with a much larger context window so that every message and tool result still fits.
Summarize or prune older turns, keep durable facts in memory, and retrieve only what each step needs.
Fine-tune the model on transcripts of past investigations so that it needs less context in each session.
explanations: The problem is a bloated input. A larger output limit does not reduce it.
A larger window postpones the limit, but cost, latency, and distraction from irrelevant content keep growing.
Context engineering curates what goes into each model call (instructions, relevant data, memory, and tool results) instead of sending everything.
Fine-tuning changes model behavior. It does not manage the growing context within a session.
takeaway: Context engineering selects, compresses, and orders the information given to a model on each call. More context is not always better context.

question: A legal team wants a model to answer questions about a 1,200-page regulatory filing. The filing is several times larger than the context window of the team's chosen model. Which approach will allow the application to answer questions accurately about the whole filing?
options: Increase the maximum output tokens so that the context window has room for the full filing.
Lower the temperature so the model uses fewer tokens per answer.
Chunk and index the filing, then retrieve only the chunks relevant to each question.
Send the whole filing in one request and rely on the model to prioritize the most relevant pages.
explanations: The context window covers input and output tokens together. A larger output allowance leaves less room for input, not more.
Temperature affects randomness, not how much input fits in the window.
RAG places only the passages relevant to each question into the context window, so any part of the filing can be used.
Input beyond the context window is rejected or truncated, so the model never sees parts of the filing.
takeaway: The context window limits the input and output tokens for one request. For large documents, chunk and retrieve (RAG), summarize in stages, or choose a longer-context model.

question: A company's AI agents need a standard, vendor-neutral way to discover and call external tools and data sources, such as a ticketing system API and a document repository, without writing a custom integration for each agent framework. Which technology is designed for this purpose?
options: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
explanations: Prompt Management stores, versions, and tests prompts. It does not connect agents to external tools.
RAG is a pattern for grounding answers in retrieved content. It is not a protocol for discovering and invoking tools.
A2A is for agents to communicate and delegate work to other agents. It is not the standard for connecting an agent to tools and data sources.
MCP is an open client-server protocol that lets agents and applications discover and call tools and access data sources in a standard way.
takeaway: MCP connects agents to tools and data. A2A connects agents to other agents. RAG is a retrieval pattern, not a protocol.

question: A company builds a financial-report assistant. A supervisor agent receives each request, delegates data retrieval to one specialist agent and analysis to another, and combines their results. Which TWO statements about this design are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: The agents share one context window, so no information needs to be passed between them.
Specialist agents with narrow responsibilities and tools are easier to test and improve independently.
Using multiple agents removes the need to evaluate the final answers.
The supervisor adds coordination steps, so each request can take longer and use more tokens than a single-agent design.
Each specialist agent must use the same foundation model as the supervisor.
explanations: Each agent runs its own model calls. Results must be passed explicitly between agents.
Separating responsibilities makes each agent's behavior simpler to evaluate, debug, and update.
Coordination adds new failure points (hand-offs, conflicting results), so evaluation is still required.
Delegation and aggregation require extra model calls, which increases latency and cost.
Agents can use different models. A smaller, cheaper model might handle retrieval while a stronger model does analysis.
takeaway: Supervisor (hierarchical) multi-agent designs are modular and specialized but add orchestration overhead, and they still need evaluation and failure handling.

question: An invoice-processing process always follows the same four steps in the same order: extract fields, validate them against a purchase order, route exceptions to a person, and post the invoice. Auditors require predictable, repeatable behavior. Which design is MOST appropriate?
options: A fully autonomous agent that decides at run time which steps to perform and in what order
A swarm of agents that negotiate which agent handles each invoice
A deterministic workflow that calls a model only for the steps that need it, such as field extraction
A single prompt that asks an LLM to perform all four steps and post the invoice
explanations: Autonomy is useful when the path is unknown. Here the path is fixed, and run-time decisions only add unpredictability.
Peer-to-peer agent collaboration adds complexity and variability with no benefit for a fixed process.
A fixed, orchestrated workflow gives predictable, auditable execution while still using a model where it adds value.
One prompt leaves validation and posting to the model without deterministic checks, which is hard to audit.
takeaway: Use agents when the steps cannot be known in advance. Use orchestrated workflows when the steps are fixed and must be auditable.

question: A travel-booking agent must remember a traveler's seat preference and loyalty number across separate conversations weeks apart. It must also keep track of details that the traveler mentioned earlier in the current conversation. Which memory design meets these requirements?
options: Fine-tuning the model on each traveler's past conversations so that it learns their preferences
A model with a larger context window, so that all past conversations can be included in every prompt
Short-term memory for the current session and long-term memory for lasting preferences
Short-term memory only, by keeping the full conversation in the prompt
explanations: Per-user fine-tuning is impractical and costly, and it bakes personal data into model weights.
Sending every past conversation is costly and slow, and it does not scale.
Short-term memory tracks the current conversation. Long-term memory stores extracted facts such as preferences for future sessions, as in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory.
Session context disappears when the conversation ends, so preferences would be lost.
takeaway: Short-term memory = within a session. Long-term memory = facts and preferences that persist across sessions.

question: A finance assistant built on an LLM gives slightly wrong totals when asked to compute statistics across a 50,000-row spreadsheet. The team needs exact results and wants to keep the conversational interface. What should the team add?
options: A higher temperature so that the model explores more possible answers
A larger model with more parameters and stronger reasoning benchmark scores
More few-shot examples in the prompt that show correct step-by-step calculations on sample rows
A code execution tool, such as AgentCore Code Interpreter, for the agent to call
explanations: More randomness makes arithmetic less reliable.
Larger models are better at reasoning but still predict tokens rather than compute exact results.
Examples can improve format and reasoning, but they do not make token prediction an exact calculator across 50,000 rows.
The model writes and runs code in a sandbox, which returns exact results that the model then explains.
takeaway: LLMs predict tokens; they are not calculators or databases. Give agents tools (code execution, APIs, queries) for exact computation and live data.

question: Which TWO use cases are the BEST fit for generative AI? (Select TWO.)
options: Detecting unusual sign-ins from a stream of authentication events
Drafting first versions of product descriptions from a list of product attributes
Forecasting next month's electricity demand from five years of hourly meter readings
Calculating sales tax on invoices by using published tax rates
Summarizing long customer support conversations for the agent who takes over the case
explanations: This is anomaly detection, a traditional ML task.
Creating new text from structured inputs is a core generative AI use case.
This is time-series forecasting on structured data, a traditional ML task.
This requires exact, deterministic calculation with conventional code.
Summarization is a core strength of LLMs.
takeaway: GenAI creates and transforms content (text, images, code, audio), summarizes, and converses. Forecasting, anomaly detection, and exact rules belong to other tools.

question: A company wants one model to draft emails, summarize meeting notes, answer questions about documents, and translate short messages, without training a separate model for each task. Which advantage of generative AI foundation models does this illustrate?
options: Determinism: the model returns the same output for the same input
Low latency: generative models respond faster than task-specific models
Adaptability: one pre-trained model can perform many tasks through prompting
Interpretability: the model shows exactly how it produced each output
explanations: Generative models are typically nondeterministic. Consistent output is not what enables multiple tasks.
Large generative models are often slower than small task-specific models.
FMs are general-purpose. The same model can switch tasks based on the instructions it receives.
Limited interpretability is a known disadvantage of FMs.
takeaway: GenAI advantages: adaptability, responsiveness, conversational interaction, and content generation. Watch-outs: hallucination, nondeterminism, interpretability, inaccuracy.

question: A customer asks a company's generative AI assistant about the return window. The assistant confidently answers "60 days," but the company's policy is 30 days, and nothing in the assistant's context mentions 60 days. What is this behavior called?
options: Data drift
Prompt injection
Nondeterminism
Hallucination
explanations: Data drift describes production inputs changing over time for a predictive model.
Prompt injection is malicious input that overrides instructions. The customer asked an ordinary question.
Nondeterminism means outputs vary between runs. The problem here is a fabricated fact.
The model produced a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by its sources and is factually wrong.
takeaway: Hallucination = confident output that is unsupported or false. Mitigate with grounding (RAG), grounding checks, and output validation.

question: A team tests a product-description generator by sending the identical prompt ten times and receives ten differently worded descriptions. The team needs outputs to be as consistent as possible for regression testing. Which change should the team make FIRST?
options: Increase the maximum output tokens.
Add a stop sequence at the end of the prompt.
Buy Provisioned Throughput so that the same model instance serves every request.
Lower the temperature (and top-p) to reduce sampling randomness.
explanations: The output limit controls length, not variation.
A stop sequence ends generation when a string appears. It does not reduce randomness.
Dedicated capacity does not remove sampling randomness.
Lower values make the model favor the most likely tokens, which reduces variation between runs.
takeaway: Sampling makes LLM output nondeterministic. Lower temperature and top-p reduce variation, although identical output is not always guaranteed.

question: A bank wants to use an LLM to recommend whether small-business loan applications should be approved. The compliance team must be able to explain precisely which factors caused each recommendation and show that the explanation reflects how the model actually decided. Which limitation of generative AI concerns the compliance team MOST?
options: Nondeterminism, because the model might give a different recommendation or wording for the same application
Toxicity, because the model might use offensive or discriminatory language in its recommendations
Limited interpretability, because its reasoning can't be traced and its explanations might not reflect how it decided
Context window limits, because applications with financial statements might be too long for the model to read at once
explanations: Variation between runs is a separate concern. The team's requirement is to explain why each decision was made.
Harmful language is a separate risk. The team's requirement is to explain the drivers of each decision.
LLM decisions emerge from billions of parameters. A step-by-step explanation is itself generated text and is not a faithful trace of the computation.
Nothing in the scenario suggests the applications exceed the context window.
takeaway: LLMs are hard to interpret, and generated explanations are not faithful traces. When faithful explanations are required, prefer interpretable models.

question: A company is preparing executives for a generative AI rollout. Which TWO statements accurately describe limitations of generative AI? (Select TWO.)
options: Foundation models automatically know about events that happened after their training data was collected.
Generative models can produce text but not images, audio, or code.
A model cannot follow instructions unless it has been fine-tuned on company data.
A fluent, confident response can still be factually wrong.
The same prompt can produce different outputs across requests.
explanations: Models know only what was in their training data. Current information must be supplied through RAG or tools.
Generative models produce text, code, images, audio, and video.
Pre-trained, instruction-tuned models follow instructions well without company-specific fine-tuning.
Hallucinations can be well written and plausible, which makes them hard to spot.
Sampling during generation makes outputs nondeterministic.
takeaway: Key GenAI limitations: hallucination, nondeterminism, limited interpretability, a knowledge cutoff, and possible bias.

question: A company is choosing a foundation model for a voice assistant in its mobile app. Users expect spoken replies to start in under one second, prompts are short, and tasks are simple, such as checking order status. Which approach BEST fits these requirements?
options: Choose the model with the largest context window so that it can hold the full conversation history.
Choose the smallest model that meets the quality bar on representative requests.
Fine-tune the largest available model so that it answers more concisely.
Choose the model with the highest score on a general reasoning benchmark to handle unexpected questions.
explanations: Prompts are short, so a large context window adds no value. Larger models are often slower and more expensive.
For simple, latency-sensitive tasks, a small model that passes your own evaluation is usually fastest and cheapest.
Fine-tuning adds cost and effort, and the large model would still respond slowly.
Top reasoning models are often the largest and slowest, and simple tasks do not need them.
takeaway: Selection criteria depend on the workload. For simple, latency-sensitive tasks, the smallest model that meets quality usually wins on speed and cost.

question: A European company must keep all inference processing for its generative AI application within EU AWS Regions. During peak hours, requests to a model in one EU Region are throttled. Which solution will increase throughput while meeting the data residency requirement?
options: Switch all interactive requests to batch inference.
Move the application to a US Region that has more capacity.
Use a global cross-Region inference profile that can route requests to any supported commercial Region.
Use a geographic cross-Region inference profile that routes requests only among EU Regions.
explanations: Batch inference is asynchronous and cannot serve interactive users.
Processing in the US violates the EU residency requirement.
A global profile can process requests outside the EU, which violates the requirement.
Geographic inference profiles spread load across Regions within one geography, which adds capacity while keeping processing in the EU.
takeaway: Cross-Region inference absorbs traffic bursts. Geographic profiles (for example, EU or US) keep processing within that geography; global profiles do not.

question: An online retailer uses generative AI to rewrite product descriptions. The retailer wants to know whether the new descriptions increase sales. Which metric MOST directly measures this business outcome?
options: Time to first token when each description is generated
BLEU score of the new descriptions compared with the original descriptions
Average number of tokens in each generated description
Conversion rate of pages with the new descriptions compared with a control group
explanations: Generation latency is an operational metric.
BLEU measures word overlap with reference text. It says nothing about sales.
Token count relates to cost and length, not to sales.
Conversion rate directly measures whether visitors buy. Comparing against a control (an A/B test) isolates the effect of the new descriptions.
takeaway: Measure GenAI with business metrics tied to the goal (conversion rate, ARPU, customer lifetime value, efficiency), ideally in an A/B test.

question: A company deploys a generative AI assistant on its customer support website. Which TWO metrics BEST indicate whether the assistant delivers business value? (Select TWO.)
options: ROUGE score of responses compared with reference answers
Number of foundation models evaluated before launch
Percentage of conversations resolved without escalation to a human agent
Average number of input tokens per conversation
Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores for conversations handled by the assistant
explanations: ROUGE is a technical text-overlap metric. It does not measure business outcomes.
This measures project effort, not business value.
Resolution without escalation shows the assistant is completing work that would otherwise cost agent time.
Token counts drive cost, but they do not show whether customers were helped.
CSAT shows whether customers find the assistant helpful, which affects retention and lifetime value.
takeaway: Tie GenAI metrics to outcomes: resolution rate, CSAT, cost per interaction, conversion, and revenue.

question: A company wants to add a generative AI chat feature to its application within weeks. It wants to try models from several providers through one API without provisioning or managing servers or GPUs. Which AWS service BEST meets these requirements?
options: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon EC2 GPU instances that run open-source models
Amazon Lex
Amazon SageMaker AI with a self-managed endpoint for each model
explanations: Bedrock is a fully managed, serverless service that provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a single API.
Self-hosting requires provisioning, scaling, and patching the infrastructure.
Lex builds intent-based conversational bots. It is not a single API to foundation models from multiple providers.
SageMaker AI gives more control but requires choosing instances and managing an endpoint for each model.
takeaway: Bedrock = serverless access to many FMs plus RAG, agents, and guardrails. SageMaker AI = build, train, and host your own models with full control.

question: A data science team wants to deploy an open-source foundation model into its own AWS account. The team must choose the instance type, run the endpoint in its VPC, and later fine-tune the model with its own training scripts. The team wants to start from a catalog of pre-trained models with one-click deployment. Which AWS offering BEST fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Amazon Quick
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference
explanations: Prompt Management stores and versions prompts. It does not deploy models.
Amazon Quick is a ready-to-use AI workspace for business users, not a model hosting tool.
JumpStart is a model hub in SageMaker AI. It deploys pre-trained and open-source models to endpoints that the team controls, and it supports fine-tuning.
Bedrock on-demand is serverless. The team cannot choose instance types or manage the endpoint.
